paras: For almost forty years, one company ran the container terminal of a large port in South America. It was the incumbent in every sense: it knew the unions, the customs officers and the regulator by name, and it had a thirty-year concession that nobody expected to change. Its business was labor-intensive and slow, but it was safe.

Then a new operator won a ten-year contract for a second terminal on the other side of the bay. Its terminal was AI-driven from the first day: automated cranes, driverless trucks and a data-heavy system that planned every move of every container. Ships that waited two days at the old terminal waited six hours at the new one. In less than three years, the new terminal had half of the market.

The old operator was not short of money or of engineers. Its problem was timing. It had studied automation for years, but it always decided that the technology was not mature yet. When it finally tried to scale up, it found a long learning curve and a workforce that did not trust the new machines. By then, its customers had already moved.

Regulators learned a lesson too. The old concession contract said nothing about automated equipment, data or cyber risk, because nobody was talking about those things when it was signed. Most experts now agree that long-term contracts need a short, flexible technology clause, reviewed every five years, so that the rules do not become obsolete before the contract does.

listenings.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the last panel of the day. The topic is technology and disruption in infrastructure, and we have a very simple format. I will ask each panelist one question, and I would like a one-minute answer. Not a five-minute speech, please. Our audience is mostly investors and public officials, so think of a short, clear answer that a busy person can repeat later. My first question is the same for everybody: in your sector, what is the one technology that will be mainstream in ten years, and who will lose if they wait too long? After that, we will open the floor for a twenty-minute question-and-answer session. Let us start with our guest from the legal side.

I ran a container terminal for twelve years, and I want to tell you about the biggest mistake of my career. We were the incumbent. We had a thirty-year concession, good relations with everybody, and a very profitable, labor-intensive business. Every year, my engineers came to me with a plan for automation, and every year I said the same thing: the technology is not ready, let us wait one more year. Then a competitor opened an AI-driven terminal across the bay, and it was not a small improvement. It was a game changer. Ships moved to them in months. When we finally decided to automate, we found a two-year learning curve that nobody had told us about. My advice is simple. You do not need to be the first. But do not be the last.
